34832994.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fluoroscopic double-contrast barium enema radiograph demonstrating pointer 4 directed at the terminal, dilated midline pelvic reservoir of the large intestine (rectal ampulla / rectum), positioned in the true pelvis anterior to the sacrum and coccyx.
34832994.keyConcept: The rectum begins at the rectosigmoid junction at the level of the S3 vertebra and terminates at the pelvic diaphragm / anorectal ring, lacking teniae coli, haustra, and appendices epiploicae.

316025890.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fluoroscopic double-contrast barium enema radiograph demonstrating pointer 5 directed at the redundant, mobile, S-shaped intraperitoneal loop of the large intestine (sigmoid colon) traversing the left iliac fossa and pelvic inlet toward the midline.
316025890.keyConcept: The sigmoid colon is an intraperitoneal segment suspended by an inverted V-shaped mesocolon (sigmoid mesocolon) that conveys the sigmoid vessels and superior rectal artery.

1382968674.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT cross-section at the T12–L1 junction displaying the liver on the right, spleen and stomach on the left, portal vein bifurcation at the porta hepatis, and the abdominal aorta immediately anterior to the vertebral body giving off the celiac trunk.
1382968674.keyConcept: The celiac trunk arises from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the T12–L1 vertebral level immediately below the diaphragmatic aortic hiatus, giving off the left gastric, common hepatic, and splenic arteries.

390785974.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT cross-section at the L1–L2 vertebral level (transpyloric plane) clearly displaying both kidneys with their renal hila and pelves, the horizontally traversing pancreatic body and tail, gallbladder fundus, and origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
390785974.keyConcept: The transpyloric plane of Addison lies midway between the jugular notch and pubic symphysis (level of L1/L2 disc) and passes through the pylorus, pancreatic neck, origin of superior mesenteric artery, renal hila, and fundus of the gallbladder.

1916690131.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical intraoral photographs of an infant demonstrating an intact upper lip with an abnormal midline fissure / cleft defect in the roof of the mouth involving the hard and soft palate.
1916690131.keyConcept: Cleft palate results from failure of the lateral palatine processes (palatal shelves) of the maxillary prominences to fuse with each other, the primary palate, and/or the nasal septum during the 7th to 10th weeks of gestation.

292982338.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical photograph of an infant demonstrating a unilateral vertical fissure / cleft of the upper lip on the left side extending toward the floor of the nostril.
292982338.keyConcept: Unilateral cleft lip is the most common congenital craniofacial anomaly, caused by failure of the maxillary prominence on the affected side to fuse with the medial nasal prominence (intermaxillary segment) during the 5th to 6th weeks of embryonic development.

83238849.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical photograph of an infant demonstrating bilateral vertical clefts of the upper lip situated on both sides of an isolated central philtrum / prolabial segment.
83238849.keyConcept: Bilateral cleft lip results from the bilateral failure of mesenchymal fusion between both maxillary prominences and the central medial nasal prominences (intermaxillary segment), leaving a protruding premaxillary prolabium.

1384160689.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intraoral clinical photograph of a protruded tongue demonstrating a prominent midline cleft / notch dividing the anterior tip and body of the tongue into two symmetrical lobes.
1384160689.keyConcept: Bifid tongue (glossoschisis) is a congenital anomaly caused by incomplete or defective embryonic fusion of the two lateral lingual swellings (derived from the first pharyngeal arch) in the ventral midline during the 4th to 5th gestational weeks.

1265327983.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical intraoral photograph of a newborn infant showing an abnormally short, thick lingual frenulum tethering the ventral tongue tip tightly to the floor of the mouth and mandibular alveolar ridge, restricting tongue elevation and protrusion.
1265327983.keyConcept: Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) results from failure of normal apoptosis and degeneration of sublingual cells during development, leaving a short, tight lingual frenulum that impairs tongue mobility and infant breastfeeding latch.

133037313.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Clinical photograph of a patient demonstrating generalized massive hypertrophy and enlargement of the tongue protruding markedly beyond the oral cavity and dental arches.
133037313.keyConcept: Macroglossia is congenital or acquired tongue enlargement often associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, congenital hypothyroidism, or Down syndrome; caused by muscular hyperplasia, vascular malformations, or lymphangiomas.

1205071122.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intraoral photograph of an open mouth demonstrating an abnormally small, rudimentary, hypoplastic tongue situated deep in the floor of the oral cavity.
1205071122.keyConcept: Microglossia (hypoglossia) is a rare congenital anomaly resulting from developmental arrest or hypoplasia of the embryonic lateral lingual swellings and tuberculum impar, frequently associated with micrognathia and limb anomalies.

1004283421.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anatomical schematic diagram illustrating the classic morphological variants of tracheo-esophageal fistula (TEF) and esophageal atresia, most prominently showing a blind proximal esophageal pouch and a distal fistulous communication connecting the trachea to the lower esophagus.
1004283421.keyConcept: Tracheo-esophageal fistula (TEF) results from defective partitioning of the foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum during the 4th to 6th gestational weeks; the most common subtype (~85%) features proximal esophageal atresia with a distal fistula to the carina/trachea.

1583622816.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Coronal cross-sectional illustration of the distal thoracic esophagus demonstrating segmental luminal narrowing / stricture with sequential passage and balloon dilation using an esophageal dilator probe.
1583622816.keyConcept: Esophageal stenosis is congenital or acquired narrowing of the esophageal lumen, embryologically resulting from incomplete recanalization of the embryonic foregut lumen during the 8th week or vascular compromise; presents with progressive dysphagia.

427969940.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Cut-away coronal schematic of the stomach and duodenum displaying massive hypertrophy of the circular smooth muscle layer of the pylorus severely narrowing the pyloric canal, with an indicator line marking the surgical pyloromyotomy (Ramstedt procedure) incision.
427969940.keyConcept: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) presents classically in first-born males at 2–6 weeks of age with non-bilious projectile vomiting, an olive-shaped epigastric mass, and hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to marked hypertrophy of the circular pyloric muscularis.

444423289.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anatomical illustration demonstrating an abnormal stomach with a deep circumferential mid-gastric constriction dividing the organ into two distinct upper and lower pouches connected by a narrow central channel (hourglass stomach deformity).
444423289.keyConcept: Hourglass stomach (bilocular stomach) is characterized by a central constriction dividing the stomach into proximal and distal compartments, typically resulting from cicatricial fibrosis and scarring secondary to chronic peptic ulcer disease along the lesser curvature.

284775126.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Coronal illustration of the lower thorax and upper abdomen demonstrating herniation / cephalad protrusion of the gastroesophageal junction and gastric cardia through the diaphragmatic esophageal hiatus into the posterior mediastinum.
284775126.keyConcept: Sliding hiatus hernia (type I) occurs when laxity or widening of the phrenoesophageal ligament allows the gastroesophageal junction and upper stomach to slide cephalad through the esophageal hiatus into the thoracic cavity, predisposing to gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

163249557.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anatomical illustration demonstrating a ring-like collar of pancreatic parenchyma completely encircling the second (descending) part of the duodenum, causing extrinsic duodenal compression and proximal duodenal bulb dilation.
163249557.keyConcept: Annular pancreas is a congenital anomaly caused by the failure of the ventral pancreatic bud to rotate properly with the duodenum during embryonic development (or persistence of a bifid ventral bud), forming a constricting ring around the second part of the duodenum that can cause duodenal obstruction.

225275816.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Embryological schematic (diagram A) demonstrating persistence of the proximal (ileal) segment of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct as a true blind-ending pouch arising from the anti-mesenteric border of the ileum, connected to the umbilicus by a fibrous band.
225275816.keyConcept: Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital GI anomaly (rule of 2s: 2% prevalence, 2 inches long, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, can contain 2 types of ectopic mucosa: gastric and pancreatic) caused by failure of the proximal vitelline duct to obliterate.

1238231216.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Embryological schematic (diagram B) demonstrating fibrous cord obliteration of both the intestinal and umbilical ends of the vitelline duct, with persistence and cystic dilation of the patent intervening middle portion (vitelline cyst / enterocystoma).
1238231216.keyConcept: A vitelline cyst (omphalomesenteric duct cyst) develops when the intermediate segment of the vitelline duct remains patent while the umbilical and intestinal ends fibrously obliterate, forming a closed fluid-filled cyst suspended between the ileum and anterior abdominal wall.

127743781.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Embryological schematic (diagram C) demonstrating complete failure of obliteration of the embryonic vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct along its entire length, producing a direct, continuous patent tubular communication between the ileal lumen and the umbilicus.
127743781.keyConcept: A vitelline fistula (umbilical-ileal fistula) results from total non-closure of the embryonic vitelline duct, creating a direct conduit between the midgut lumen and the exterior that classically presents with neonatal fecal discharge from the umbilicus.
